limitations_and_boundaries: Differences in bile acid signaling properties between human and mouse may hamper translational conclusions.
Less abundant or characterized bile acid metabolites may complicate interpretation.
Individual variations in microbiota may affect response to bile acid-derived drugs.
The role of intestinal FXR signaling modulation in humans after bariatric surgery remains to be demonstrated.
Interaction between FXR and specific macronutrients warrants further investigation.

research_questions.statement: How does the gut microbiota modulate bile acid signaling via FXR and TGR5, and what is the impact on host metabolism?

provenance.text_excerpt: Speciﬁcally, they observed that Tempol decreased the genera Lactobacillus and Clostridium (clusters IV and XIV), which was accompanied by decreased BSH activity and accumulation of intestinal TbMCA.

claims.statement: Tempol alters gut microbiota composition (decreases Lactobacillus and Clostridium), leading to decreased BSH activity, accumulation of TβMCA, and suppressed FXR signaling.

provenance.text_excerpt: Thus, we demonstrated that the microbiota regulates both the metabolism and the synthesis of bile acids in an FXR-dependent manner (Sayin et al., 2013).

claims.statement: The gut microbiota regulates bile acid synthesis in an FXR-dependent manner by reducing the FXR antagonist TβMCA, thereby increasing FXR signaling and inducing Fgf15 expression.

experiments_or_tasks: Measurement of bile acid composition and FXR signaling in germ-free (GF) vs conventionalized mice (Sayin et al., 2013).

provenance.text_excerpt: Thus, a picture emerges that FXR may have beneﬁcial effects on chow diet, whereas on high-fat diet, Fxr-deﬁciency may protect against metabolic disease, in particular, when intestinal FXR is inhibited.

claims.statement: FXR effects on metabolism are context-dependent: beneficial on chow diet but FXR-deficiency may protect against metabolic disease on high-fat diet, particularly when intestinal FXR is inhibited.

provenance.text_excerpt: Thus, intestinal and hepatic FXR may have opposing effects on steatosis.

claims.statement: Intestinal and hepatic FXR have opposing effects on steatosis: hepatic FXR protects against steatosis, while intestinal FXR deletion protects against steatosis on high-fat diet.

provenance.text_excerpt: In contrast, experiments with Tgr5-deﬁcient mice showed that TGR5 did not contribute to the reduced body weight, increased energy expenditure, or increased glucose-stimulated insulin secretion after vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG) (McGavigan et al., 2015).
